html:
The Fourth Lateran Council was a gathering of the Catholic Church in Rome in November 1215, called by Pope Innocent III and attended by some four hundred bishops and many other clergy. It was the largest Church council of the Middle Ages.

It passed seventy decrees. Every Catholic was to confess and take communion at least once a year. The doctrine of transubstantiation, that bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, was defined. Rules were set for clergy conduct, for marriage banns, and against clergy taking part in trials by ordeal, which helped end that practice. Heresy, such as that of the Cathars, was condemned, and the council backed the Albigensian Crusade in southern France.

It also ordered Jews and Muslims to wear distinctive dress, a rule that fed later persecution. A new crusade to the east was planned, which became the Fifth Crusade in 1217. The council confirmed Innocent's claim of papal power over rulers in Europe, at the peak of medieval papacy. Its decrees shaped Catholic life for centuries.
